what_its_for: Ofloxacin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections, including urinary tract infections (UTIs), pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), skin infections, pneumonia, bronchitis, sexually transmitted infections like gonorrhea and chlamydia, and eye infections. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It will NOT work for colds, flu, or other viral infections.
how_to_take: Take ofloxacin tablets by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). You may take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help prevent an upset stomach. Try to take it at the same times each day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body. Always finish your full course of antibiotics, even if you start feeling better — stopping early can allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe the right dose and length of treatment based on your type of infection, how serious it is, and your kidney function. Common adult doses range from 200 mg to 400 mg taken every 12 hours (twice a day) for 3 to 14 days, depending on the infection. Never take more or less than prescribed. Do not share this medication with others.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Store ofloxacin tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids containing aluminum or magnesium, calcium supplements, iron supplements, multivitamins with minerals, or sucralfate (Carafate) within 2 hours before or 2 hours after taking ofloxacin, as they can prevent the medicine from working properly. Avoid caffeine, as ofloxacin can make caffeine's effects stronger. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and tanning beds — ofloxacin makes your skin more sensitive to sunlight, so use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or lightheaded. Avoid alcohol as it may worsen side effects like dizziness.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden or worsening tendon pain, swelling, or a snapping feeling in any joint (especially the ankle, heel, or shoulder) — this could signal a tendon tear; numbness, tingling, or weakness in your arms or legs; serious mood changes, confusion, hallucinations, or thoughts of hurting yourself; a severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; fast or irregular heartbeat; signs of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, rapid heartbeat); severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody; difficulty breathing or swelling of the face, lips, or throat (signs of allergic reaction). Also tell your doctor if your symptoms do not start improving after a few days.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 1 to 3 days of starting ofloxacin, but it is very important to take the full course of treatment prescribed by your doctor. Just because you feel better does not mean the infection is completely gone. Stopping early can cause the infection to return and be harder to treat.
special_populations: Children and Teenagers: Ofloxacin is generally NOT recommended for patients under 18 years old because it may affect developing joints and cartilage. Older Adults (65+): Use with extra caution — older adults have a higher risk of tendon problems and heart rhythm changes. Kidney Problems: Your doctor may lower your dose if your kidneys are not working well, since ofloxacin is removed from the body through the kidneys. Pregnancy: Ofloxacin is not recommended during pregnancy due to potential risks to the baby. Talk to your doctor about safer alternatives. Breastfeeding: Ofloxacin passes into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before using it while breastfeeding.
